# Question 1, Part B: Creating MaxBrShare {#sec-q1b}

## Creating the variable (item 4)

For household $i$, define $\mathrm{MaxBrShare}_i = \max_{b \in B} s_{ib}$, where $B$ contains the eight named brands and $s_{ib}$ is brand $b$'s share of that household's total purchase volume. This measures concentration on a named brand, irrespective of its identity, which is the loyalty perspective needed for the purchase-behaviour segmentation.

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-create

# Check the named-brand inputs before calculating a maximum. Do not hide missing shares.
q1b_named_shares <- soap_raw |> select(all_of(brand_cols))
stopifnot(all(vapply(q1b_named_shares, is.numeric, logical(1))),
          all(is.finite(as.matrix(q1b_named_shares))),
          all(as.matrix(q1b_named_shares) >= 0),
          all(as.matrix(q1b_named_shares) <= 1))

soap <- soap_raw |>                                      # retain all original household information
  rowwise() |>                                          # calculate separately for each household
  mutate(MaxBrShare = max(c_across(all_of(brand_cols)))) |> # take the largest of its eight named shares
  ungroup()                                             # restore ordinary, ungrouped operations
```

The calculation is row by row because the required maximum belongs to each household, whereas a column maximum would describe a brand across different households. `BrOthers` is excluded because it pools several small brands, so its combined share cannot identify loyalty to any single brand. The named shares retain their original total-volume denominator and are not renormalised. The `mutate()` call adds the new variable to the household data, and `ungroup()` removes the row-wise grouping.

## Checking the variable (item 5)

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-summary

# Inspect the distribution with summary().
summary(soap$MaxBrShare)

# Fail clearly if any household has a missing, infinite or out-of-range result.
stopifnot(nrow(soap) == nrow(soap_raw),
          all(is.finite(soap$MaxBrShare)),
          all(soap$MaxBrShare >= 0 & soap$MaxBrShare <= 1))
```

The observed minimum is `r min(soap$MaxBrShare)` and the maximum is `r max(soap$MaxBrShare)`, and all `r nrow(soap)` households pass the range and completeness checks. The median is `r scales::percent(median(soap$MaxBrShare), accuracy = 0.1)`: half the households allocate no more than this share of their volume to their most-purchased named brand.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-zero-households
#| tbl-cap: "Brand count and pooled-brand share among households with MaxBrShare equal to zero."

# Isolate the households with no recorded volume in any named brand.
q1b_zero_households <- soap |> filter(MaxBrShare == 0)

# Count their observed combinations without assuming that all zero households are alike.
q1b_zero_profile <- q1b_zero_households |>
  count(NoBrands, BrOthers, name = "households")

q1b_zero_profile |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(NoBrands = "Number of brands purchased", BrOthers = "BrOthers share",
             households = "Households") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = BrOthers, decimals = 0)
```

There are `r nrow(q1b_zero_households)` such households (`r scales::percent(nrow(q1b_zero_households) / nrow(soap), accuracy = 0.1)` of the sample). Their recorded `NoBrands` values are `r paste(sort(unique(q1b_zero_households$NoBrands)), collapse = ", ")`, and their `BrOthers` shares are `r paste(scales::percent(sort(unique(q1b_zero_households$BrOthers)), accuracy = 0.1), collapse = ", ")`. These households purchase one brand outside the eight named brands: excluding the pooled category leaves eight zero shares, whose maximum is zero. Consequently, a zero here means no concentration on a **named** brand, rather than no purchases or no brand loyalty. Treating these households as disloyal would misdirect loyalty promotions.

## Repeating the distance calculation (item 6)

Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences. A smaller value indicates greater similarity. With `MaxBrShare` as the only coordinate, the distance is simply the absolute difference between the two households' maximum shares.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-example-shares
#| tbl-cap: "The toy households with their maximum brand share added."

# Add the loyalty measure to a local copy, preserving the shared example for Part A.
q1b_example <- brand_example |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(MaxBrShare = max(c_across(c(BrandA, BrandB)))) |>
  ungroup()

q1b_example |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Household = "Household", BrandA = "Brand A share",
             BrandB = "Brand B share", MaxBrShare = "Maximum brand share") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(BrandA, BrandB, MaxBrShare), decimals = 2)
```

Households X and Y each concentrate `r scales::percent(q1b_example$MaxBrShare[q1b_example$Household == "X"], accuracy = 1)` of volume on one brand, while Z's largest share is `r scales::percent(q1b_example$MaxBrShare[q1b_example$Household == "Z"], accuracy = 1)`. The measure therefore represents concentration rather than the name of the brand bought.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-distance-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Euclidean distances using the original two shares and MaxBrShare alone."

# Recompute the Part A baseline from the supplied data, without needing Part A's object names.
q1b_raw_matrix <- q1b_example |> select(BrandA, BrandB) |> as.matrix()
rownames(q1b_raw_matrix) <- q1b_example$Household
q1b_raw_distances <- as.matrix(dist(q1b_raw_matrix, method = "euclidean"))

# Use ONLY MaxBrShare for the new distances, as required by item 6.
q1b_loyalty_matrix <- q1b_example |> select(MaxBrShare) |> as.matrix()
rownames(q1b_loyalty_matrix) <- q1b_example$Household
q1b_loyalty_distances <- as.matrix(dist(q1b_loyalty_matrix, method = "euclidean"))

# Extract each distinct pair once, retaining labels for the comparison.
q1b_distance_comparison <- tibble(
  first = c("X", "X", "Y"), second = c("Y", "Z", "Z")
) |>
  mutate(pair = paste(first, second, sep = " / "),
         raw_shares = q1b_raw_distances[cbind(first, second)],
         maximum_share = q1b_loyalty_distances[cbind(first, second)]) |>
  select(pair, raw_shares, maximum_share)

q1b_distance_comparison |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(pair = "Household pair", raw_shares = "Original brand shares (Part A)",
             maximum_share = "MaxBrShare alone (Part B)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(raw_shares, maximum_share), decimals = 3)
```

In the Part A representation, X and Y are `r sprintf("%.3f", q1b_raw_distances["X", "Y"])` apart, while X/Z and Y/Z are each `r sprintf("%.3f", q1b_raw_distances["X", "Z"])` apart, so the equally concentrated households appear most different. Using `MaxBrShare` alone makes X/Y's distance `r q1b_loyalty_distances["X", "Y"]` and each distance to Z `r q1b_loyalty_distances["X", "Z"]`, correctly identifying X and Y as equally loyal in terms of purchase concentration. This resolves the particular representation problem in @sec-q1a, but deliberately discards brand identity: the original shares would still be useful for a question about which brand households favour.

## Reading MaxBrShare with NoBrands (item 7)

`MaxBrShare` describes concentration on the most-purchased named brand, while `NoBrands` records how many brands a household buys, so the two provide complementary evidence about loyalty. Reading them together also prevents a household that buys only one small brand within `BrOthers` from being labelled disloyal merely because its `MaxBrShare` is zero.

## Additional validation and interpretation

### An independent calculation

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-second-method

# pmax compares corresponding positions across the eight columns without row-group overhead.
q1b_vectorised_max <- do.call(pmax, as.list(q1b_named_shares))

# Verify equality of the full result vectors, rather than only their summaries.
q1b_methods_agree <- all.equal(soap$MaxBrShare, q1b_vectorised_max)
q1b_methods_agree
stopifnot(isTRUE(q1b_methods_agree))
```

The two methods agree for every household (`r isTRUE(q1b_methods_agree)`). The row-wise method makes the required household-level operation explicit. The vectorised `pmax()` calculation is the more efficient form for this repeated numeric operation because it works across whole vectors without creating a separate row group for each household. This is an explanation of computational overhead, rather than a claim based on a timing benchmark.

### Distribution of concentration

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1b-maxbrshare-histogram
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the largest named-brand share across households."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Use fixed-width bins on the natural share scale.
ggplot(soap, aes(x = MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = pal[1], colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
  labs(title = "Concentration on a named brand varies across households",
       x = "Largest share of purchase volume in one named brand", y = "Households")
```

The middle half of households lie between `r scales::percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.25), accuracy = 0.1)` and `r scales::percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.75), accuracy = 0.1)`. A total of `r sum(soap$MaxBrShare == 1)` households allocate all recorded volume to one named brand. This spread supports distinguishing concentrated buyers from households that spread volume more widely, while the zero group needs the pooled-brand qualification above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1b-maxbrshare-nobrands
#| fig-cap: "Maximum named-brand share against brand count. Points may overlap. The line connects the median at each observed brand count."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Summarise concentration within each brand count without changing the shared data.
q1b_by_brand_count <- soap |>
  group_by(NoBrands) |>
  summarise(median_share = median(MaxBrShare), .groups = "drop")

# A deterministic scatter plot avoids adding random jitter to the shared seeded pipeline.
ggplot(soap, aes(x = NoBrands, y = MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[1], alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(data = q1b_by_brand_count, aes(y = median_share),
            colour = pal[2], linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(soap$NoBrands))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Brand count and concentration describe loyalty",
       x = "Number of brands purchased", y = "Largest named-brand share")
```

Households with the same brand count can have different maximum shares, so brand count alone does not reveal how evenly purchases are spread. The single-brand households also include both named-brand buyers at the upper end and the pooled-brand households at zero. A client should therefore consider brand breadth and concentration together before choosing a retention or switching promotion. This plot describes an association and does not establish the effect of a promotion.

### Do the nine shares total approximately one?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-share-total-check
#| tbl-cap: "Checks on the sum of the eight named shares and BrOthers."

# Match the absolute tolerance used by the shared setup, without changing any source shares.
q1b_share_tolerance <- 0.01
stopifnot(is.numeric(soap$BrOthers), all(is.finite(soap$BrOthers)),
          all(soap$BrOthers >= 0 & soap$BrOthers <= 1))
q1b_share_totals <- soap |>
  select(MemberID, all_of(brand_cols), BrOthers) |>
  mutate(share_total = rowSums(pick(all_of(brand_cols), BrOthers)),
         deviation = share_total - 1)

# Keep exceptions identifiable by household ID for checking against the source data.
q1b_share_exceptions <- q1b_share_totals |>
  filter(abs(deviation) >= q1b_share_tolerance) |>
  select(MemberID, share_total, deviation)

q1b_share_totals |>
  summarise(households = n(), minimum_total = min(share_total),
            maximum_total = max(share_total),
            outside_tolerance = sum(abs(deviation) >= q1b_share_tolerance)) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(households = "Households", minimum_total = "Smallest total",
             maximum_total = "Largest total", outside_tolerance = "Outside tolerance") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(minimum_total, maximum_total), decimals = 6)
```

Using an absolute tolerance of `r q1b_share_tolerance` around one, `r nrow(soap) - nrow(q1b_share_exceptions)` households pass and `r nrow(q1b_share_exceptions)` fall outside the tolerance. Therefore, the statement that every household's shares sum to approximately one is not supported at the tolerance used in the shared setup.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-share-exceptions
#| tbl-cap: "Source-data households outside the share-total tolerance."

q1b_share_exceptions |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(MemberID = "Household ID", share_total = "Sum of nine shares",
             deviation = "Total minus one") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(share_total, deviation), decimals = 6)
```

These totals range from `r sprintf("%.6f", min(q1b_share_totals$share_total))` to `r sprintf("%.6f", max(q1b_share_totals$share_total))`. The exceptional records are retained as supplied: renormalising would change the measure specified in Question 1 and conceal the data-quality issue. `MaxBrShare` still passes its range checks, but loyalty conclusions for these records should be treated cautiously until their shares can be checked against the original transactions.
